paper_title: Refer-CityFlow and M3Track: A Benchmark Dataset and Reference Framework for Language-Driven Multi-Target Multi-Camera Tracking
paper_abstract: Referring multi-object tracking enables users to specify targets through natural language, but existing Refer-MOT benchmarks primarily focus on single-camera settings. We formalize Referring Multi-Target Multi-Camera Tracking (Refer-MTMCT), where free-form queries specify identity-consistent trajectories to be recovered across a network of sequential, sparse-overlap cameras. We introduce Refer-CityFlow, a benchmark built on CityFlow's global cross-camera identity annotations and augmented with language queries requiring joint language grounding, cross-camera association, and spatio-temporal reasoning. Refer-CityFlow covers 96 videos from 40 roadside cameras with 660+ identity-consistent cross-camera trajectories, 4,362 trajectory-level descriptions, and 7,699 queries, including 1,699 real-user queries collected from 50 participants. Reference experiments on the four-camera Scenario 02 show that single-camera referring trackers reach 14.95-18.28 HOTA on real-user queries, while the evaluated cross-view method achieves about 0.05 HOTA in direct transfer. To establish reference performance, we provide M3Track, a modular multimodal reference framework in which a large language model (LLM)-based agent orchestrates interchangeable detection, tracking, and cross-camera association modules. M3Track reaches 44.10 HOTA and 65.40 IDF1 on the same real-user query set. The project repository is available at https://github.com/phuongnguyen194/Refer-CityFlow-and--M3Track.
comments: Accepted for publication at the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV 2027), Evaluations and Datasets Track. 10 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables

paper_title: Phantom Consensus: Measuring Social Reasoning in Multi-Agent LLM Decision-Making
paper_abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly aggregate judgments across model instances, but reasoning about other agents can itself introduce failure. We study a setting in which LLMs shift their public decisions after observing ambiguous social signals while reporting inaccurate estimates of what other agents privately judged, even when the group's recorded private judgments do not support the apparent consensus. We call this failure phantom consensus and study it as a pluralistic-ignorance-style pattern in controlled LLM collectives. To measure this phenomenon, we introduce PHANTOM-Bench, a benchmark that separates isolated private judgments, public decisions after ambiguous social signals, elicited estimates of the group's private judgment, transparency-based recovery, and controls for neutral public text and explicit vote-following. Across nine closed- and open-weight models, ambiguous public signals consistently degrade decision quality and can turn correct private group judgments into incorrect public collective outcomes. Public accuracy drops by as much as 47.8 percentage points, and collective rationality failures reach 47.3% in the most susceptible setting. We observe substantial errors in reported group-private beliefs alongside public-stage failures, while control conditions reveal model-dependent differences in susceptibility to ambiguous and explicit peer signals. Revealing the agents' recorded private decisions repairs many failures without revealing the gold label, although recovery varies across models. Our results show that evaluating multi-agent LLM systems requires measuring not only final agreement, but whether that agreement reflects independently measured private judgments or an apparent consensus.

paper_title: Flex-RSI: Benchmarking Recursive Self-Improvement of Frontier Agents
paper_abstract: Frontier language models are increasingly deployed as agents, and how well an agent performs depends not only on its model but also on its harness: the prompts, tools, memory, and control loop through which the model acts. When an agent is applied to a new problem, a natural question is whether it can use the feedback of the task to improve the way it works, and not merely its answer. Most existing benchmarks keep the agent's harness fixed and score the solution it produces, or target large-scale model training. We introduce Flex-RSI, a benchmark for the recursive self-improvement of agents on vision and robotics tasks under a fixed budget. In each round, an executor improves the task solution, which is kept only if it scores higher on held-out validation data, and an improver then revises the harness, including the executor and itself. Every run starts from the same general-purpose harness, and the final solution is scored on hidden test data. Evaluating closed-source and open-weight models on tasks spanning perception, reasoning, robot action, 3D reconstruction, visual creation, and infrastructure, we find that self-improvement helps most when the agent builds its own solution, that feedback recording only success or failure holds back open-weight models, and that open-weight models fall furthest behind where outputs must pass strict checks of physical stability or exact correctness. Paired runs further show that editing the harness itself contributes to the gains.
comments: Project page: https://flex-rsi.github.io. Jingdong Zhang and Jionghao Wang contributed equally

paper_title: Ordered Policy Optimization
paper_abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) stabilizes policy updates by clipping the importance ratio between the new policy and the data-collecting policy. The standard rule uses one fixed clipping range for all samples. While this choice offers simplicity and effectiveness, it fails to distinguish statistically harmful extreme ratio values from large, yet tolerable changes. We study how to adapt the clipping radius to the reliability of the induced importance ratio distribution. Our case study demonstrates that reliable updates require controlling these extreme ratios, rather than merely verifying that individual ratios fall within a fixed interval. Motivated by this observation, we propose Ordered Policy Optimization (\textsc{OPO}). In each minibatch, \textsc{OPO} sorts the importance ratios, selects the extreme ratios that potentially have the largest effect on the update, and assigns them adaptive sample-wise radii instead of using the fixed clipping radius. These radii are derived from a prescribed tail profile, which specifies desired target values for the selected extreme ratios. The resulting objective remains first-order and requires only minibatch sorting and a modified policy loss. Experiments conducted on MuJoCo and Atari benchmarks demonstrate that this simple modification achieves strong performance relative to established baselines.
comments: 36 pages, 12 figures, 11 tables. Published in Proc. of the 40th Conference on Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

paper_title: DRAFT-Bench: Evaluating Frontier Agents Across the Professional Design Lifecycle
paper_abstract: Can frontier general-purpose agents understand client intent, explore creative directions, execute revisions, and prepare production deliverables? We introduce DRAFT-Bench (Design Reliability Across Feedback and Tasks), a lifecycle-oriented evaluation of requirement elicitation, creative exploration, constrained editing, iterative revision, and production handoff. Its Requirement-to-Artifact framework links evolving requirements, protected properties, artifact versions, and delivery obligations. We compare native Codex/Astra and Claude Code across 35 design briefs under 43 conditions, alongside a separate 40-scenario RFQ track. Astra completes 43/43 design conditions and Claude 35/43. All scored core runs receive full structural credit, yet on the 28 core conditions scored for both systems, semantic checks flag violations in 11 for Astra and 5 for Claude; these are model judgments, not expert-confirmed failure rates. RFQ coverage is high, but success ordering changes across cohorts. SKU expansion, revision dependencies, and White ink files expose ambiguity among unmet obligations, missing inputs, and evaluator interpretations. These findings separate execution, requirement compliance, and professional acceptance. Unpaired tracks and different tools preclude claims of RFQ-to-delivery success, factory acceptance, or a pure model ranking.

paper_title: Grid-Oriented Probabilistic Load Forecasting for AI Data Centers
paper_abstract: Probabilistic load forecasts for AI data centers need to represent both uncertainty under changing workloads and temporal dependence to support grid operations. This paper develops an open, grid-oriented benchmark using measured GPU power from a 448-GPU AI cluster. Forecasts are evaluated through four stages: probabilistic prediction, online uncertainty calibration, temporal scenario generation, and horizon-wide reserve sizing. Following a change in cluster utilization, a quantile LightGBM forecast achieves only 63.4% coverage for a nominal 90% interval, while online regime-conditioned calibration increases coverage to 87.3%. Even with well-calibrated marginal forecasts, independent sampling produces unrealistic ramp distributions and excessive reserve procurement. Reconstructing temporal dependence from historical forecast errors reduces the discrepancy in ramp statistics and lowers realized reserve cost by 7.4-10.6% across three forecasting tasks. These findings show that marginal forecast quality alone is insufficient for operational decisions and motivate joint evaluation of calibration, temporal structure, and decision outcomes.

paper_title: Frame: Form-Restricted Authoring with Model-Based Evaluation
paper_abstract: Many professional reports reuse the structure of prior editions while updating the content. We formalize this setting as form-restricted report generation: given a sample report and new grounding documents, generate a report that preserves the sample's form while accurately reflecting the new evidence. We introduce FRAME, a benchmark of 120 EDGAR- and arXiv-derived instances across Financial Quarterly, Financial Annual, Academic Simple, and Academic Complex categories, built with a temporal three-snapshot pipeline. We evaluate outputs with three human-validated metrics: structural similarity via semantic tree-edit distance, coverage via information unit recall, and faithfulness via claim-level grounding verification. Across five LLMs, open-source models nearly match proprietary models on structure but lag on coverage and faithfulness; all models perform better on financial than academic reports, and performance declines with longer outputs and more complex grounding.

paper_title: Composable Causality: A Toolkit for Systematic Time-Series Causal Discovery and Treatment-Effect Benchmarking
paper_abstract: Real-world multivariate time series rarely come with verified ground-truth causal structure, so research on time-series causal discovery and treatment-effect estimation depends on synthetic data. Existing tools are either fixed datasets that cannot be modified after release or script-based generators in which each script fixes one combination of mechanism, confounding, and missingness. Neither supports controlled experiments that vary a single property, such as sparsity, noise distribution, or missingness mechanism, while holding the others fixed. Counterfactual evaluation has the same gap, since existing simulators are built per paper with hardcoded mechanisms or produce observational data only. We introduce DTCD (Datasets and Toolkit for Causal Discovery), a data generation library that produces multivariate time series with ground-truth contemporaneous and lagged adjacency matrices. Topology, mechanism, noise, observational mask, and intervention policy are independent components that compose through configuration alone. Paired counterfactual twins, produced by caching the stochastic realization during the factual rollout and re-injecting it during the interventional rollout, recover individual treatment effects to numerical precision. A reference benchmark of eight discovery algorithms on eighty-one configurations and four treatment-effect estimators on eighteen configurations exposes failure modes that aggregate metrics hide. These include the inability of standard discovery methods to handle missing values, regardless of whether the missingness mechanism is informative, and a marginal-variance shortcut (varsortability) that we measure and remove by standardization. Code and data: https://github.com/hferdous/Composable_Causality
comments: 30 pages, 10 main text pages plus references and appendices, with figures and tables. Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets Track. Code and data at https://github.com/hferdous/Composable_Causality

paper_title: HomeLoop: A Simulation Framework and Benchmark for Robot-IoT Coordination in Everyday Domestic Assistance and Safety
paper_abstract: Recent progress in embodied robotics is bringing robots closer to deployment in homes, as vision-language models (VLMs) are demonstrating significant advances in reasoning, making VLM-driven robots promising home assistant agents. These agents will often be introduced into homes that already have cameras, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and residents with wearables. To fulfill their potential, they need to integrate with existing smart infrastructure and reason through ambiguous scenarios: a smoke alarm may come from a pan about to ignite, a pan already on fire, a resident cooking or a faulty sensor, and each calls for a different response. To that end, we introduce HomeLoop, a simulation framework and benchmark built on Isaac Sim that combines robot bodies, networked devices and wearables, simulated residents and visitors, faulty sensors, and hazards that evolve over time. Our benchmark is composed of 20 tasks across five families grounded in real-world household hazards and needs, and designed so that the same alert can have different causes. A runtime monitor scores each episode with temporal-logic checks on the final outcome and the actions along the way, and every action carries a predefined cost. We evaluate six open-weight and proprietary VLMs. The best achieves a family-balanced score of 61.9%, and across models we see a pattern of over-reaction: failed episodes involving prohibited interventions outnumber those involving missed required interventions by more than two to one, with models often shutting off the stove before investigating the alarm's cause. HomeLoop is an extensible foundation intended for use in research on robot-IoT coordination, long-term memory, proactive assistance, and privacy-safety trade-offs. HomeLoop will be released with 2,100 home layouts that can be automatically furnished in diverse configurations, five robot bodies and 20 networked device types.

paper_title: SSF-Net: A Spatial-Spectral Fusion Network for Accurate PDE Operator Learning
paper_abstract: Machine learning methods for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) significantly improve computational efficiency over traditional numerical solvers such as finite element method (FEM). However, PDE dynamics inherently span both local and global dynamics: disturbances propagate and decay gradually through the domain, while global coupling effects can influence the whole system simultaneously. Capturing both types of dynamics with a low complexity model remains a key challenge. To address this, we propose the Spatial-Spectral Fusion Network (SSF-Net), built around a dual-branch Spatial-Spectral Fusion (SSF) block comprising a spatial branch and a spectral branch. The spatial branch employs a multi-directional Mamba, which mitigates its inherent causal, single-direction scanning bias and capture local interactions with reduced directional bias at linear complexity. The spectral branch leverages a Fourier transform with a block-diagonal MLP to efficiently capture global spectral features with reduced parameter count and complexity. The SSF block is embedded in a multiresolution convolutional encoder-decoder, which extracts multi-scale features. We evaluate SSF-Net on a comprehensive PDE benchmark spanning multiple task types and assess its long-horizon stability. Compared with attention-based and convolution-based baselines, SSF-Net achieves lower prediction error with fewer parameters while retaining near-linear asymptotic complexity in the number of spatial tokens.

paper_title: An Evaluation of Zero-Shot Classification of Multimodal Foundation Models for Point Clouds
paper_abstract: Modelling the existing building stock for maintenance, renovation, and decommissioning relies on point clouds from laser scanning or photogrammetry, whose objects must be segmented and classified, traditionally with computer vision models that require task-specific training. To avoid this training, this paper proposes to use the zero-shot classification capabilities of multimodal foundation models (MMFMs) for the pre-classification of segmented point clouds. Our approach renders one to four isometric views of each object and classifies them with MMFMs. Weevaluate it on the public datasets ModelNet40 and S3DIS Area 5 across several MMFMs. OnModelNet40, the best configuration, Gemini-3.6-Flash with four views, achieves 55.4% accuracy and a Macro-F1 of 47.7%, and all six MMFMs evaluated with one to four views improve as the number of views increases. On S3DIS, adding textual dimensions derived from an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) to the RGB views improves the accuracy of all four evaluated models; for Gemini-3.6-Flash, accuracy increases from 42.1% to 60.5% with a Macro-F1 of 59.7%. While MMFMs remain below specialised trained classifiers, they show that MMFMs can support the zero-shot pre-classification of segmented point clouds and could support bootstrapping the annotation of training data. The evaluation framework is publicly available on GitHub.

paper_title: Modeling AI-Driven Industry–Education Integration as a Socio-Technical System: A Synergetic Four-Dimensional Collaborative-Efficacy Evaluation Framework
paper_abstract: Industry–education integration (IEI) is organized as a socio-technical system in which universities, enterprises, students, and artificial intelligence co-produce learning outcomes. Its collaborative efficacy, however, has remained unmeasured, because the elements of the system are assessed in isolation. Grounded in Haken’s synergetics, this paper models AI-driven IEI as a four-dimensional collaborative system (University, Enterprise, Student, and AI; UESA). It defines collaborative efficacy as a super-additive, emergent property rather than a weighted average of parts. The UESA framework operationalizes the system through 27 tertiary indicators aggregated into a single efficacy function V. Indicator weights are set by the analytic hierarchy process (AHP) and revised by Bayesian posterior correction as operational data accumulate. The framework is implemented on an operational industry–education integration platform, which couples a large language model (DeepSeek), a job–curriculum knowledge graph, and a topological recommendation engine. In an A/B trial of 3000 undergraduates, enabling the AI layer raised all four system dimensions. The largest gains were in student competency adaptability (+26.0) and AI enablement (+22.9). All 12 key tertiary indicators improved at p < 0.01, and overall efficacy V rose from 64.0 to 83.3. The results indicate that collaborative efficacy in a socio-technical IEI system is measurable and dynamically adaptive, and that it can be decomposed into the contributions of its constituent subsystems.

paper_title: Quality and Authenticity Evaluation of Condiments Using Near-Infrared Spectroscopy: A Critical Review
paper_abstract: Condiment matrices are chemically complex, and seasonings of different categories suffer from batch-to-batch variations and high risks of adulteration. Conventional physicochemical titration and chromatographic methods involved laborious sample pretreatment and long assay durations, which hindered their applications for on-line production monitoring and large-scale commodity screening. Combined with chemometrics, near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) had enabled rapid, non-destructive and simultaneous multi-parameter analysis, and had emerged as a vital tool for condiment quality assessment. This review had systematically summarized research advances of NIRS in condiment analysis, covering quantitative determination of physicochemical properties, authentication and adulteration detection, geographical origin tracing, and on-line monitoring of fermentation processes. Key bottlenecks restricting industrial implementation had been discussed, including spectral overlap interferences derived from complex matrices, limited sensitivity toward trace constituents, poor model transferability across instruments, and the absence of unified industrial standards and shared spectral libraries. Prospects had been proposed from the perspectives of multi-modal data fusion, spectral interpretation algorithms, full-supply-chain quality traceability, and standardization, providing theoretical support and references for the technical upgrading and large-scale industrial implementation of rapid condiment detection.

paper_title: Evaluation of Lettuce (Lactuca sativa L.) Genotypes for Resistance to Lettuce Drop Caused by Sclerotinia minor Jagger
paper_abstract: Lettuce drop caused by Sclerotinia minor Jagger is among the most economically important diseases affecting lettuce production worldwide. The present study aimed to evaluate the response of 51 lettuce genotypes originating from the gene banks of the Institute of Plant Genetic Resources, Sadovo, Bulgaria, and the Centre for Genetic Resources (CGN), Wageningen, the Netherlands, to artificial infection with S. minor. Field experiments were conducted during 2025 and 2026 under open-field conditions. Plants were inoculated with isolate 35A of S. minor, and survival rates were assessed 30 days after inoculation. Significant differences among genotypes were observed regarding their response to pathogen infection. No immune genotypes were identified. The highest survival rates were recorded for the genotypes Lollo Rossa, Bianka, Belokriska-16260 and Therna Gyumurdjaska-13312, which were classified as slightly susceptible. These accessions may serve as valuable sources of partial resistance in future breeding programs. The results confirm the scarcity of highly resistant lettuce germplasm and emphasize the necessity of integrating genetic resistance with other disease management strategies.

paper_title: A Structured Review of Distributed Quantum Computing: Infrastructure, Protocols, Applications, Compilation, and Security
paper_abstract: Distributed quantum computing (DQC) connects quantum processing units (QPUs) to execute programs beyond the capacity of a single processor. Understanding its scalability requires examining the interactions between hardware, communication, software, and security. This structured review synthesizes 126 studies, mainly published between 2020 and 2026 with foundational earlier work, retrieved from eight sources and selected using documented inclusion and exclusion criteria. We organize the literature into five pillars: infrastructure, protocols, applications, compilation, and security. A common scoping rule distinguishes work enabling distributed computation from broader quantum communication research. The synthesis identifies interconnect rate and fidelity, classical control latency, remote-operation overhead, and coherence constraints as coupled limits on distributed execution. Infrastructure and protocol research includes experimental demonstrations, whereas application and compiler evaluations remain predominantly simulation-based. Security requires both protected interconnects and confidential, verifiable delegated computation. Comparisons across the pillars reveal tradeoffs between local computation, communication resources, sampling overhead, and trust assumptions. The review highlights unresolved challenges in distributed fault tolerance, transduction, interoperable software, benchmarking, and integrated security. Its central conclusion is that scalable DQC requires coordinated hardware–software–network design and evaluation of complete systems rather than isolated improvements within individual layers.

paper_title: World Models for Digital Agents: An Agent-Centric Survey
paper_abstract: Digital agents operating in software-defined environments, including games, web interfaces, mobile GUIs, tool-use systems, and code repositories, often benefit from anticipating the consequences of actions before execution. World models provide a principled mechanism for such anticipation, but their utility in digital settings is neither automatic nor uniform. Unlike physical environments, digital transitions are interface-mediated and program-governed, and the value of prediction depends less on perceptual realism than on preserving functionally relevant consequences for downstream decisions. This survey presents the first dedicated agent-centric treatment of world models across major digital-agent domains. We introduce a unified design space, W = (X , L, U), organized around three complementary questions: what is modeled, how predictive capability is built, and how world models are used inside the agent loop. Through this lens, we synthesize a rapidly growing literature spanning semantic transition models, visual and latent simulators, tool-state predictors, executable code-based world models, and hybrid predictive systems. We further examine environments, datasets, and evaluation protocols as a coupled empirical pipeline, and highlight open challenges, notably the persistent gap between predictive fidelity and downstream utility.

paper_title: Comparing MSME Development Across BRICS Economies After GDP Rebasing: Methodological Challenges for Empowerment Policy Evaluation
paper_abstract: Introduction: GDP rebasing and national-accounts revisions can improve the visibility of informal and MSME activity, but they also alter data sources, classifications, estimation procedures and the comparability of economic series. The supplied literature further indicates that GDP alone is insufficient for evaluating empowerment, enterprise performance and distributional outcomes. Methods: The researcher selected Google Scholar and ERIC as databases and information sources. The eligibility protocol limited publications to 2015–2026. The verified identification provenance did not record the exact calendar date of search execution; this differs from the publication-year eligibility range. We searched Google Scholar and ERIC using a prespecified Boolean strategy for studies published from 2015 to 2026. The recorded PRISMA workflow identified 150 records, removed 62 duplicates, screened 88 records, assessed 60 full texts and included 59 records. Results: Rebasing can broaden MSME visibility through newer surveys, administrative data and size-sensitive supply-use or input-output tables, but revised estimates are not automatically comparable across time or countries. Informality, unpaid work and non-observed activity remain central measurement gaps. The evidence supports multidimensional indicators covering income, employment, survival, household welfare, gender, productivity, sustainability and environmental effects. Transparent metadata, data governance, methodological validation and institutional capacity are enabling conditions. We found no direct, consistent comparisons of post-rebasing empowerment outcomes across all five BRICS economies. Discussion/Conclusion: GDP rebasing is best understood as an institutional measurement reform rather than a self-sufficient evaluation of MSME empowerment. Its policy value depends on transparent revisions, harmonised definitions, improved coverage of informal activity and complementary enterprise- and welfare-level indicators.

paper_title: Genetic Evaluation of IL12B and ITGB7 Therapeutic Pathways in Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Implications for Childhood Bone Health
paper_abstract: Genetic evaluation of therapeutic targets can clarify disease-pathway relevance and developmental compatibility in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). We performed two-sample drug-target Mendelian randomization using cis-pQTL instruments for IL12B and ITGB7, evaluating IBD, Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, and childhood total-body bone mineral density (BMD), with pediatric total-body-less-head BMD replication. Four IL12B and two ITGB7 instruments were retained. Higher genetically proxied IL12B abundance was associated with IBD (OR, 1.341; 95% CI, 1.280–1.405), Crohn disease (OR, 1.357; 95% CI, 1.278–1.441), and ulcerative colitis (OR, 1.339; 95% CI, 1.262–1.420), whereas ITGB7 showed no convincing disease association. Neither target showed convincing evidence of a major effect on childhood BMD; replication was inconclusive, with lower precision for ITGB7. Primary colocalization showed no supportive evidence of a shared causal signal; IL12B–IBD strongly favored distinct signals (H3 = 0.999995; H4 = 5.07 × 10⁻⁶). Exploratory fine-mapping suggested possible sharing with a secondary IBD component, but this finding was prior-sensitive and limited by LD-reference reliability. Bayesian analyses were compatible with small IL12B BMD effects, whereas ITGB7 remained less precise. Overall, these findings support IL12B-related pathway relevance while informing developmental compatibility rather than drug efficacy or clinical safety.

paper_title: Autonomous Space Systems via Reinforcement Learning: Review, Challenges, and Future Directions
paper_abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly being investigated for spacecraft guidance, navigation, control, and mission autonomy, particularly where uncertainty, nonlinear dynamics, limited onboard computation, or changing operating conditions challenge conventional approaches. This review examines RL and closely related learning-based methods across major space-control applications, including attitude and orbit control, low-thrust and cislunar guidance, planetary landing, small-body operations, rendezvous and docking, space robotics, surface mobility, and mission-level autonomy. Reported results are assessed with respect to classical baselines, quantitative performance, robustness, computational cost, and validation fidelity from simulation to hardware and flight demonstrations. Across the literature, learned controllers often show advantages in adaptation, robustness to modeled uncertainty, and rapid onboard evaluation, while numerical optimization and classical control generally retain advantages in nominal optimality, interpretability, and established guarantees. Hybrid architectures, in which learning modifies or augments a conventional guidance or control law, provide some of the most consistent results. Important limitations remain in out-of-distribution generalization, benchmarking, statistical reporting, navigation realism, verification, implementation assurance, and independent high-fidelity validation. The review concludes with proposed benchmark problems, reporting practices, and a staged validation pathway for assessing learned controllers in increasingly realistic space-system environments.

paper_title: Auditable Evaluation Protocol for Spam Detection Under Bounded Paraphrase Attacks
paper_abstract: Spam-filter scores are difficult to interpret when split construction, attack denominators, and candidate validity are not retained. We evaluate an auditable RMF-PC protocol using word and character TF-IDF views, structural cues, calibrated fusion, and an optional paraphrase-consistency gate. The protocol freezes data, fitting, attacks, predictions, and review decisions; separates deterministic L1 rewrites from human-adjudicated L2/L3 candidates; and keeps exact-deduplicated Track A distinct from group-near-deduplicated Track B. On Track A (seed 42), gated RMF-PC achieved clean F1 97.937%, L1 F1 98.117%, and L1 spam FNR 1.971% (11/558). Its FNR difference from linear SVM was -0.538 percentage points (exact McNemar p=0.5078; paired-bootstrap 95% interval -1.613 to +0.538), so superiority is unresolved. On Track B, the same comparison had a raw p=0.0215 but a Holm-adjusted p=0.0859, showing that cohort policy can affect an inferential conclusion. Two reviewers and adjudication retained 38 L2 and 55 L3 candidates; observed misses were 1/38 and 0/55. Enron and third-party Zenodo-curated TREC tracks show corpus sensitivity and fixed 5%/10% adaptation results. Findings are limited to the retained local protocols.

paper_title: The Protocol is the Result: How Evaluation Choices Flip the Verdict on Lightweight Image Restoration
paper_abstract: Lightweight image restoration is infrastructure: student-scale super-resolution and low-light enhance-ment models are re-implemented, compared and reported on constantly. Their reported numbers are, however, not directly comparable, because the evaluation protocol is rarely stated in full. We decompose the protocol into five operational dimensions and measure each of them on a matrix of 21 protocol cells across three tasks and five random seeds (105 evaluations in total). On the ×4 super-resolution task the choice of protocol moves the reported metric by 3.889 dB—and by 19.794 dB once best-of-60 cropping is included—which is 4.98 times the 0.782 dB gain the trained model achieves over its bicubic reference. The effect is not statistical noise: seed-to-seed variation accounts for 0.49–0.93%of the protocol span on that task. Switching off the antialias flag of the downsampling operator—a single boolean, with the same weights, the same images and the same code path—moves the model’s gain over bicubic from +0.818 dB to −1.753 dB, reversing the verdict. We also find that the claim is conditional rather than universal: on low-light enhancement the protocol span is only 0.21 times the training gain, because that task has far more headroom. Finally, a coding of 63 recent papers shows that only one states its aggregation method, none states its validation batch size, and of the 15 papers whose validation and test sets can be judged from the text, none states whether those sets coincide (the other 48 were not coded, since deciding it needs the code or the appendix). We close with six reporting requirements that would remove the ambiguity.

paper_title: Resilient Consensus Under Time-Varying Delays and Adversarial Agents: Safety, Rates, and Delay-Induced Equivocation
paper_abstract: Trimming-based consensus rules such as weighted mean-subsequence-reduced (W-MSR) consensus protect multi-agent networks against a bounded number of faulty or malicious agents, but most of their guarantees assume synchronous, delay-free communication. Real networks deliver delayed, reordered, and replayed messages, and timestamps cannot be trusted when adversaries can forge them. For resilient consensus with bounded delays, prior work shows that (F+1, F+1)-robustness is necessary and (2F+1)-robustness is sufficient. To our knowledge, whether the gap between the two conditions is real has remained open. We study a timestamp-free W-MSR rule in which every normal agent trims received values relative to its own current state while neighbor values arrive with arbitrary time-varying delays bounded by τ. First, we prove a safety property that holds for every adversary and every delay pattern: the hull of normal states over the most recent τ+1 steps never expands. Second, we prove that (2F+1)-robustness suffices for exponential consensus, with a contraction horizon of |N|(τ+1)+τ steps that is linear in τ+1. Third, we show that (F+1, F+1)-robustness is not sufficient once delays can be scheduled adversarially: with τ=1, a broadcasting adversary can present different recent values to different receivers and block consensus on a family of graphs that, by exhaustive enumeration, is (F+1, F+1)-robust for F ≤ 2 and 2F-robust for F ≤ 3. We also specify a reproducible simulation protocol built on certified robust graphs, three delay schedules, and four adversary models including stale replay. This preprint presents the model, the analysis, and the evaluation protocol. It does not report empirical outcomes.

paper_title: Transmission Expansion Investment Evaluation Considering the Impact of Behind-the-Meter Generation
paper_abstract: Behind-the-meter (BTM) generation and energy communities reduce the demand that transmission networks must carry, yet expansion planning still treats that demand as given. This paper examines transmission investment when demand growth, including new large loads such as data centres, is supplied behind the meter instead of being connected directly to the transmission grid. BTM self-supply is represented as a virtual transmission resource, a nodal reduction of net demand, in static and multi-period mixed-integer linear expansion models with a DC network representation, and a BTM Index (BTMI), which covers individual self-generation and energy communities, ranks the nodes where BTM deployment should be promoted. Applied to the Garver system and the Colombian 500 kV backbone, the methodology shows that the required transmission capital expenditure decreases as BTM penetration grows, and that part of it is postponed: in Colombia a 5 % penetration removes 30 % of the base plan, a 30 % penetration removes 88 %, and final penetrations of 10 % and 20 % reduce its present value by 27.5 % and 53.7 %. The reduction occurs in steps, depends on where the resource is located and is bounded by the connection of new load. Future assessments should add the N-1 criterion and both the night-time peak and the daytime high-solar condition.

paper_title: An Explainable Dance Pose Evaluation System Using Velocity-Adaptive Filtering and Dynamic Alignment
paper_abstract: Practicing dance from pre-recorded online tutorials allows students to learn motor skills independently, yet learners frequently struggle without an instructor to identify technical errors. This paper addresses the research problem of objective, monocular video dance evaluation by developing an end-to-end computer vision framework that compares a student’s practice video with an instructor’s reference recording. Our methodology extracts 33 body landmarks, normalizes coordinates by torso length to account for body differences and camera distances, and applies a velocity-adaptive Kalman filter that eliminates lag during fast steps while preserving stability during held poses. A Dynamic Time Warping module with a ±0.25 s tolerance window evaluates body posture without penalizing expressive musical timing. Continuous routines are segmented into discrete poses using feature-divergence tracking, with a rule-based engine outputting plain-language postural corrections. The system was evaluated across 15 full-body benchmark routines comprising 10,550 video frames from the AIST Dance Video Database and instructional exercises in both frontal and 90◦ side views. The results demonstrate that the system tracks fast direction changes accurately, detects technique breakdowns reliably, and matches professional instructor ratings closely (r = 0.88, Mean Absolute Error = 4.8 points). In conclusion, this automated framework offers accessible, actionable feedback for home physical education using standard consumer cameras.

paper_title: Where and Why is Grounded Reasoning Useful?
paper_abstract: Grounded reasoning, where a model outputs text coordinates of relevant locations in chain-of-thought reasoning, is a common strategy for solving complex visual reasoning problems. However, the benefits and limitations of grounded reasoning are understudied. We study where and why grounded reasoning is most useful. To do so, we introduce a chain-of-thought analysis method to measure how much a model uses its outputted grounding in its thinking trace and perform a detailed ablation study of a grounded reasoning training recipe. We find that grounded reasoning improves counting but shows no significant gain over baselines without coordinate grounding across a wide range of spatial reasoning and perception benchmarks. Using several synthetic tasks, we show that grounded reasoning is most useful when a task requires undescribable references, which are visual concepts that are difficult to describe in language. However, we observe that many existing visual reasoning benchmarks are solvable with only describable text references. To close this gap, we introduce BrickVision, a new benchmark that requires undescribable visual references to solve.

paper_title: XStack: A Benchmark for ML Repo Migration
paper_abstract: ML code should run where researchers choose, not where it was first written. Today, machine learning code mainly lives in two ecosystems, PyTorch on NVIDIA GPUs and JAX on Google TPUs. Migrating repositories between them means building and testing across frameworks and hardware. This migration is (1) a practical need, since it unlocks different hardware for researchers, and (2) a natural benchmark: it involves different frameworks and hardware, covers whole repositories, and is long-horizon and challenging. We introduce XStack, a benchmark that evaluates agents on migrating ML repositories between these two ecosystems. Each agent receives a PyTorch repository and a clean TPU machine and must deliver a JAX repository. Its output passes if it meets our grading criteria, based on the source repository's published result, authenticated and calibrated by us. Migration by agents remains unreliable: Claude Opus 5 passes 75%, GPT-5.6-sol 45%, and every other agent at most 40%. XStack is a step toward freeing ML code from its ecosystem. We release XStack to make progress toward reliable migration across frameworks and hardware measurable.

paper_title: A Hidden Markov Preference Model for Online Prediction of Adversary Actions
paper_abstract: A defender anticipating an attacker needs a probability distribution over the attacker's next action from information available before that action occurs. Two structures complicate this: the attacker's behavioral regime persists and can switch within an episode, and each action combines an operation with state-dependent arguments whose feasible values change over time. We capture both with a hidden Markov model whose latent state is the active regime and whose regime-conditioned action law is defined on a feasibility-masked tree of executable actions. The same likelihood forms the next-action distribution and updates the regime belief once the action is seen, and a partially observed prefix contributes its resolved local factors. Estimation separates into convex logistic fits that Baum-Welch reuses when regimes are unlabeled. We derive a reach-weighted nodewise KL expression for regime information, a sequence-wise log-loss bound for switching regime paths, and a uniform fallback guarantee. On the CAGE 2 cyber defense benchmark the filtered latent state is worth 0.8 nats per step, and after a controller switch the loss begins to fall in three steps against ten for a recurrent baseline.

paper_title: SM4RT: Cascaded Feed-forward Model for 4D Reconstruction
paper_abstract: We introduce SM4RT, a multi-task cascade feed-forward model for dynamic scene reconstruction from RGB videos. While existing feed-forward approaches typically address geometry reconstruction and motion estimation separately--and often predict motions in a single coordinate frame that must account for camera movement--SM4RT solves these tasks sequentially by first reconstructing 3D geometry and then bootstrapping motion estimation from the predicted structure. By expressing each pixel's 3D motion in its corresponding camera frame, SM4RT reduces ambiguity arising from camera motion. To address the sparsity of real-world motion labels, SM4RT further incorporates a weakly supervised loss that regularizes unlabeled point motions using labeled point positions at the other time step. We evaluate motion estimation on three dynamic-scene datasets--Kubric, Waymo, and Point Odyssey--and SM4RT achieves the best performance on most metrics compared with prior baselines. We additionally benchmark geometry reconstruction on five dynamic scene datasets and show that SM4RT achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods. Overall, our unified framework demonstrates that combining geometry reconstruction and motion estimation in a cascade not only avoids performance trade-offs but also enhances motion estimation through improved geometric reasoning.

paper_title: Data-driven discovery of intrinsic Lie point symmetries of differential equation systems
paper_abstract: Discovering continuous symmetries directly from differential-equation data can reveal geometric structure for model reduction and scientific machine learning without symbolic determining equations or a closed-form representation of the governing system. We formulate intrinsic Lie point-symmetry discovery as an operator-theoretic problem on sampled jet-space data. Admissible generators are identified from a sampled determining operator and separated from redundant, solution-dependent, and geometrically trivial directions. The framework combines prolongation, sequential subspace restrictions, and a fixed nonlinear dictionary linear in trainable coefficients. A rank-stabilization preflight test diagnoses systems whose represented intrinsic symmetry algebra does not stabilize under dictionary refinement. On a controlled differential-equation benchmark with an analytically known 11-dimensional represented intrinsic symmetry algebra, the method recovers the complete represented generator set, reproduces its Lie-bracket structure to numerical precision, and approximates a known generator beyond the training domain. Here we show that explicit intrinsic continuous-symmetry generators can be recovered from data obtained from exact or approximate differential systems.
comments: 63 pages, 10 figures. Code and data availability statements are included in the manuscript

paper_title: On the limitations of molecular representations
paper_abstract: Molecular representations such as fingerprints and learned embeddings play a central role in cheminformatics and small-molecule machine learning. They serve as the primary input for a diverse array of tasks, including clustering, dataset splitting, and virtual screening, yet their evaluation is often limited to downstream model performance on narrow benchmark tasks. We carried out a systematic investigation of the quality of molecular representations, finding that none of the state-of-the-art molecular embedding models capture graph structure, 3D shape, or ADMET endpoint similarity better than fingerprints or physicochemical descriptors. However, classical fingerprints also revealed their own material limitations. For example, we show that depending on the representation, between 225M and $\sim$4B molecules have non-unique representations in the 10.8B Enamine REAL database, with implications for virtual screening. Our findings provide an insight into the current limitations of molecular representations, outlining future research directions for the development of more robust encodings of small molecules.

paper_title: Benchmarks as Software: Terminal-Bench and the Case for Continuous Benchmarks
paper_abstract: Coding agents are among the most economically consequential deployments of LLMs to date, making reliable evaluation increasingly important. Yet even benchmarks that are carefully validated at release can become stale. As models improve, they can discover valid solutions that existing verifiers reject, while changes to evaluation infrastructure can invalidate assumptions embedded in tasks and tests. We call the resulting accumulation of defects benchmark maintenance debt: a growing gap between benchmark scores and the capabilities they are intended to measure. We introduce a continuous-validation workflow for agentic benchmarks that combines community reports, task artifacts, agent traces, automated oracle checks, and human-gated repairs. We apply this workflow to Terminal-Bench 2.0, a benchmark that underwent extensive human and LM-assisted review and red-teaming before release. Our audit identifies issues in roughly 30% of the benchmark, and we release the resulting repairs as Terminal-Bench 2.1. These repairs change evaluation results: accuracy increased by over 10 percentage points and leaderboard positions move by up to three ranks, even as the overall ranking remains highly correlated (Spearman rho = 0.958).   We evaluate how resource allocation shapes benchmark conclusions. We show that fixed wall-clock can materially change agent performance: For example, extending the time limit closes a 20pp harness gap on GPT 5.4 and shrinks a 30 pp gap on GPT 5.4 mini to 5 pp. Benchmark maintenance is therefore not only about repairing task artifacts: resource budgets are part of the measurement specification and must be validated alongside the tasks themselves.   More broadly, benchmark maintenance debt is not just accumulated implementation bugs: our results show that as models improve, both evaluation assumptions and resource settings may need to be revalidated.

paper_title: Social Humanoid: Socially Responsive Human-Humanoid Interaction
paper_abstract: Humanoid robots are typically trained as solitary agents, leaving them unable to coordinate physically with human partners who naturally anticipate and adjust to one another. To bridge this gap, we present Social Humanoid, a hierarchical system that generates and executes socially responsive whole-body motion on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 conditioned on a human partner's motion. Its high-level policy performs flexible sequence modeling of human and humanoid motion through a shared tokenized representation, generating reactive humanoid motion and anticipating the partner's motion when they are occluded, while a low-level whole-body tracking controller executes the generated motion on the robot. To train the system, we introduce a two-phase adaptive retargeting procedure that retargets one interaction partner to the robot while morphing the other partner to preserve contact dynamics, reachability, and relative body scale. We apply this procedure across five motion-capture datasets to produce a new Human-Humanoid Interaction (HHI) benchmark of 260 hours of human-humanoid interactions. Our results demonstrate that Social Humanoid produces coordinated, human-aligned behavior across diverse interaction types in simulation and the real world. Project page: https://von31.github.io/social-humanoid/

paper_title: StepBack: Step-Level Error-Localized Resampling for Efficient Test-Time Reasoning
paper_abstract: Self-consistency (SC) is a widely used decoding strategy for improving chain-of-thought reasoning, but it requires sampling many complete reasoning trajectories with a preset budget. Its efficient variants reduce the cost mainly by stopping full-trajectory sampling early or distributing the number of samples across questions. In this paper, we propose StepBack, a step-level error-localized resampling method for efficient test-time reasoning. Given a small set of draft trajectories, StepBack localizes likely first error positions using lightweight signals and then resamples the detected error step and its suffix, followed by majority answer voting. Empirically, StepBack matches the accuracy of SC on average across seven mathematical reasoning and multi-hop QA benchmarks, while reducing token usage by up to 41.26%. In addition, by nature, StepBack can be combined with adaptive inference methods such as Adaptive Consistency, further improving their inference-time efficiency.

paper_title: Synthesis of Ovarian Cancer Multi-Omics Datasets: A Biology-Informed Evaluation Framework
paper_abstract: Paired multi-omic cancer cohorts are costly to assemble and difficult to share, motivating synthetic cohorts as a complementary resource. As generative model development accelerates, we shift the focus from proposing yet another architecture to defining evaluation criteria that determine whether synthetic data preserve biologically relevant structure. We introduce a biology-informed and patient-disjoint framework for evaluating the generation of paired RNA expression and copy-number variation (CNV) profiles, and apply it to the longitudinal DECIDER high-grade serous ovarian cancer cohort. The framework assesses modality-specific fidelity and coherence between RNA and CNV pairs using agreement between real training and held-out data as a reference, alongside complementary training-data proximity diagnostics. We adapt three multi-omic integration architectures based on variational autoencoders to generate paired profiles. The model leading several fidelity and coherence measures also shows the strongest training-data proximity. The protocol and case study offer the community a reference for comparing future multi-omic generators.
comments: Accepted at the GenAI4Health Workshop at NeurIPS 2026 and in the Findings track of ML4H 2026. Both acceptances are non-archival

paper_title: Adaptive Low-Light Enhancement for Road Anomaly Detection: A Multi-Architecture Benchmark and Edge Deployment Study
paper_abstract: Road anomaly detection systems on autonomous vehicles must function reliably under degraded visual conditions including darkness, rain, and Harmattan dust haze. This paper benchmarks four object detection architectures, YOLOv8n, YOLOv12n, RT-DETR, and Faster R-CNN, under physically grounded lighting and weather degradation, and shows that uniform application of the SCI low-light enhancement network is actively harmful at dusk-level lighting (-16.1% to -30.7% mAP@50). We propose a lightweight, training-free luminance-adaptive router that selects between no enhancement, moderate SCI, and denoising plus strong SCI based on per-frame Rec. 601 luminance, recovering most of the dusk penalty while preserving low-light gains, and we validate the full pipeline on NVIDIA Jetson Nano edge hardware.

paper_title: Hybrid Machine Learning for Imbalanced Landing-Phase Safety Event Prediction from Flight Data
paper_abstract: Landing-phase safety-event prediction requires the detection of rare abnormal approaches within strongly imbalanced multivariate flight data. Capturing coupled temporal behavior while distinguishing event-specific signatures across airport operating contexts remains a central modeling challenge. This study proposes an interpretable hybrid feature-fusion framework for multiclass landing-phase safety-event prediction. A long short-term memory (LSTM) autoencoder trained on nominal flight windows characterizes deviations from routine approach behavior. Its continuous reconstruction-error descriptor is fused with parameter-specific statistical flight-history features and supplied to a class-weighted XGBoost classifier to distinguish Normal, Speed High, Path High, and Flaps Late windows. The framework is evaluated using 53,750 NASA DASHlink approach windows from three arrival airports. Pooled and airport-specific learning strategies are compared alongside component-level benchmarks, repeated pipeline retraining, and feature-attribution analysis. The results demonstrate strong class-balanced detection, with mean macro recall above 0.90 across all airports under repeated partitioning and retraining. Component comparisons establish the importance of class weighting and show that continuous feature fusion outperforms reconstruction-error-only and hard-gate alternatives. Airport-level comparisons reveal benefits from local specialization at the two airports with larger datasets and from pooled training at the airport with the smallest dataset. Feature attributions associate predictions with operationally relevant vertical-path, configuration, speed, and approach-context variables. The framework provides an interpretable approach to rare-event detection and practical guidance for adapting flight-data monitoring models to airport-level data availability.

paper_title: Module-Aware Optimization for Graph Neural Networks
paper_abstract: Different optimizers impose different geometries on parameter updates. Adaptive methods such as Adam and AdamW use coordinate-wise updates, while matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon utilize weight-matrix structure through orthogonalized updates. For Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), however, the effective geometry of its weight matrices is shaped not only by its learned channel-mixing weights, but also by the graph-propagated representations it acts on. Thus, even if an update is well normalized as a matrix, its effect on the layer output can be amplified when applied to graph-propagated features. To address this gap, we introduce GraphMuon, a graph-aware optimizer that adapts Muon's matrix updates to the covariance structure of graph-propagated layer inputs. GraphMuon performs orthogonalization in a metric defined by these propagated representations and normalizes step sizes according to the update's induced effect on the layer representation. We show that theoretically, vanilla Muon can suffer from graph-induced update amplification, while our GraphMuon can mitigate this effect. As such, our GraphMuon yields a graph-metric analogue of Muon's polar update step. Empirically, GraphMuon achieves $1.32\times$-$2.42\times$ validation-loss time-to-target speedups over AdamW on three large-scale OGB benchmarks. Across 15 dataset-architecture configurations spanning node classification, inductive graph classification, and graph regression, it achieves lower time-to-target in 13 cases, while maintaining competitive or superior predictive performance. Code is available at https://github.com/guy-hadad/GraphMuon.

paper_title: NPCBench: A Clinical Apprenticeship Benchmark for Multimodal Care-Pathway Reasoning in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma
paper_abstract: Current medical benchmarks typically break down clinical competence into isolated factual questions, single-image tasks, or static case vignettes. These tests score individual answers, but reveal less about whether a model can integrate subspecialty knowledge with multimodal evidence and track a patient's condition throughout a course of care. To close this gap, we introduce NPCBench, a clinical apprenticeship benchmark for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). NPCBench mirrors specialist training, from guideline and foundational knowledge to case planning, longitudinal review, CarePath integration, and open-ended consultation. It contains 4,777 component and consultation items and a 100-patient CarePath cohort with 417 scored diagnostic and care tasks. The episode-level evaluation tests whether diagnostic and care answers are jointly correct within a care pathway. By linking stepwise tasks to patient-level care trajectories, NPCBench evaluates whether models ground decisions in visual evidence, interpret changes in patient state, and meet clinical requirements in consultation. Across 30 evaluated models, we observe a composition gap: strong performance on individual tasks does not ensure jointly correct diagnostic and care answers for the same patient. Among 21 multimodal models, strict CarePath success reaches at most 23%. Paired controls and physician calibration further examine evidence grounding, longitudinal revision, and consultation judging. Overall, NPCBench broadens the evaluation of medical artificial intelligence beyond static question-answering paradigms to an apprenticeship-oriented assessment of clinical workflows, thereby offering a testbed for evidence-based and temporally coherent reasoning in oncology care.
comments: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026), Evaluations and Datasets Track

paper_title: USB Gym: A Gymnasium Testbed for Closed-Loop Ultrasound View Matching
paper_abstract: Background and Objective: Our main goal is ultrasound guidance: moving a probe until its image matches a target view. Published methods for each part of a guide are evaluated in separate simulators. We asked whether these methods, combined into one guide, are good enough.   Methods: We built USB Gym, a testbed whose standard engine simulates ultrasound from public patient CT, with a network drawing organ textures from CT labels. Its guide has three replaceable parts (slots), an organ segmenter, a controller and a reward, which received 20 published methods, each run on the same 60 episodes of six held-out patients. In each slot, a published method replaced ours only if detectably better on these patients. The better of this combination and our original guide on 20 new CTs is the benchmark baseline. A pose oracle, reading the exact probe pose available only in simulation, set the reference. The results below are exploratory.   Results: On these CTs, the probe started on average 16.0 mm from the target view; the pose oracle brought it to 1.5 mm. Of the results known when the combination was fixed, only an image-similarity reward (SSIM) was slightly but detectably better, so the combination was our guide with that reward. This combination was the benchmark baseline, ending at 13.7 mm (16% of the oracle's progress).   Conclusions: Combining untuned published methods with ours did not guide the probe near the target view; the task remains under-explored. The testbed accepts new methods; no guide was tested on hardware.
comments: 75 pages; supplementary material (62 pages) as an ancillary file. Submitted to Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine. Code: https://github.com/tohnperfect/USBGym

paper_title: Learning the Task or Learning the Verifier? Rethinking Criteria Exposure in Embodied Self-Improvement
paper_abstract: Self-improving embodied agents are increasingly being developed and compared on robot simulation benchmarks. Several recent works expose the benchmark's success criteria to the learning agent, a practice we call Criteria Exposure (CE). These criteria, originally written to verify policies trained by imitation learning, often demand more than the corresponding language instructions, so a score from such a verifier may not faithfully reflect whether the instructed task was completed, especially for robot-control programs written by an agent. As embodied coding agents report ever higher benchmark scores, a natural question arises: when a coding agent is exposed to the benchmark's criteria, does it generate code that better performs the instructed task, or code that simply overfits to the verification criteria? We conduct controlled experiments with a self-improving agent with and without CE, and find that with CE the agent quickly produces code with a higher success rate under the given criteria, but this advantage disappears when the criteria are changed slightly without departing from the original instructions. More importantly, the skills the agent develops under CE transfer poorly across tasks. We further propose instruction-faithful criteria and show that they better reflect the performance of agent-generated programs.

paper_title: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Heterogeneous Cognitive and Biomedical Knowledge Graphs: The Role of Graph Grounding in Multi-Hop Reasoning and Hallucination Mitigation
paper_abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in biomedical and cognitive neuroscience, but their ability to reason reliably over heterogeneous knowledge graphs (KGs) remains unclear. We benchmark five LLMs (GPT-5.1, Gemini 2.0 Pro, Llama 3, Qwen, and BioGPT) across five KGs: DrugBank, NeuroSynth, Cognitive Atlas, Brain Map, and GDPKG. We introduce a multitier query dataset to evaluate reasoning depth and factual accuracy under KG-aware (graph-grounded) and KG-agnostic conditions. Inter-annotator agreement was substantial, with Cohen's kappa of 0.781 (range: 0.753-0.807) and Fleiss' kappa of 0.77. Results show that general-purpose models, particularly GPT-5.1 and Gemini 2.0 Pro, generally outperform domain-specific models on multi-hop and high-level reasoning tasks, although performance declines as query complexity increases. KG grounding reduces hallucination rates across all evaluated models. Contrary to our initial hypothesis, domain-specific models do not consistently outperform general-purpose models on specialized tasks without graph grounding. These findings highlight the value of combining broad language-model capabilities with structured domain knowledge. We provide practical guidance for selecting LLM-KG integration strategies based on task complexity and computational constraints, and discuss hybrid neurosymbolic architectures for personalized medicine, cognitive disorder diagnosis, and explainable AI.

paper_title: Measured Coupling for Parallel Decoding in Diffusion Language Models
paper_abstract: Diffusion language models can write many tokens per step, but must choose which tokens are safe to commit together. Mean-field decoding penalizes pairs of positions whose predictions look alike. We replace this proxy with the coupling itself: how much committing one token changes the model's confidence at another. Cheap probes inside the main forward pass measure it, with no training or extra model, and it plugs into the same mean-field rule. On three models and four benchmarks, our method needs far fewer steps than mean-field decoding and is faster in most settings, also with a key-value cache, at an average accuracy cost of 1.1 points. Shuffling the couplings or replacing them with a uniform bonus loses this gain.

paper_title: AutoCompress: Automated Hardware-Guided Model Compression
paper_abstract: LLM pruning must preserve quality while meeting hardware- and workload-specific constraints on latency, throughput, and memory. Existing pruning workflows often target parameter counts, requiring practitioners to manually select model sizes that meet latency, throughput, and GPU memory limits. However, parameter count alone does not predict these metrics, which depend on the model architecture, workload, hardware, and serving engine. We introduce AutoCompress, a hardware-guided compression framework that directly incorporates such constraints into differentiable architecture search. AutoCompress jointly optimizes global and per-layer structure to produce heterogeneous architectures, guided by serving-engine cost models validated against end-to-end latency, throughput, and memory measurements. We evaluate AutoCompress on long-context local coding, batched datacenter serving, and latency-sensitive in-game interaction. Compared to the state-of-the-art Minitron pruning framework, AutoCompress improves average accuracy across eight benchmarks by 6.57, 2.35, and 0.57 percentage points on RTX 5070, RTX 5080, and H100, respectively. AutoCompress also compresses Nemotron 3.5 Super from 120B to 74B parameters for single-B200 BF16 serving at 128K context, retaining 95% of its mean benchmark score.

paper_title: Interactive Visual Gym: Evaluating Visual Interaction Models with Simulated Users in Interactive Worlds
paper_abstract: Visual interaction models that support users during ongoing physical tasks require evaluation in closed loop, where assistant responses can change subsequent user behavior and task outcomes. Existing benchmarks largely rely on offline replay and therefore cannot capture these effects. We introduce Interactive Visual Gym, a framework for closed-loop evaluation and training of visual interaction models through joint simulation of executable task environments and human users. We contribute three simulators that recreate everyday tasks and human-aligned action spaces across cooking, household manipulation, and mobile-interface domains, together with a persona-conditioned user simulation harness that collaborates with the assistant while incorporating controlled execution errors and other out-of-plan behaviors. We instantiate the framework as IVG-Bench, a benchmark with 315 interaction scenarios. Evaluating state-of-the-art VLMs as visual interaction models reveals substantial limitations: the best-performing model, Gemini 4 Argon, completes only 53.4% of tasks within the time limit, exhibits significant weaknesses in factual grounding and actionable guidance, and is often too slow to prevent errors when response latency is considered. We verify our evaluation protocol with a human study which finds 78.5% agreement between our interaction-quality metric and participant preferences. We further show that the environments provide useful learning signals: in a proof-of-concept GRPO experiment, closed-loop training improves both task success and interaction quality for Qwen3.5-4B model in our cooking environment.

paper_title: LeanContext: Disentangling Mathematical Resources from Local Formal Context in Lean Whole-Proof Generation
paper_abstract: Neural theorem proving increasingly uses retrieved premises and project context to support proof generation. Evaluating these resources requires measuring the advantage of target-selected declarations over comparable alternatives and how this advantage depends on training. We introduce LeanContext, a benchmark of 129,826 Lean whole-proof generation problems, to investigate these questions. We group selected complete preceding mathematical declarations as Mathematical Context (MC) and the remaining selected local source commands as Environment Context (EC). Four aligned input views support crossed training and inference evaluations with shared targets and original Lean verification environments. For both diffusion- and autoregressive-based models, selected declarations outperform comparable alternatives by a larger margin when training includes MC. Final-input audits identify omitted declarations referenced by the target. Prioritizing these dependencies improves Pass@32 by 1.40% and 1.70% for LLaDA and Llama, respectively, on 2,000 targets. The selection experiment operates without access to target reference proofs and holds checkpoints, EC, and inference budgets constant. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/haaaardcvZ/LeanContext.

paper_title: SplatAnything: Gaussian Spacing Normalization for Feed-forward 3DGS across Arbitrary Scenes
paper_abstract: We identify a key limitation of existing feed-forward 3DGS methods: Gaussian attributes are typically predicted in a radial-distance-normalized space that canonicalizes a global radial statistic of the reconstructed geometry, while the spacing between neighboring Gaussian centers can still vary substantially across scene scales and camera configurations. This mismatch induces systematic shifts in Gaussian-scale targets, leading to ambiguous supervision. To address this, we propose SplatAnything with Gaussian Spacing Normalization (GSNorm), which canonicalizes a robust scene-level statistic of Gaussian spacing to provide a more consistent spatial reference for Gaussian prediction. To rigorously assess our method, we further establish a systematic benchmark spanning diverse datasets, input sparsity levels, and challenging extrapolated viewpoints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SplatAnything achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly strong gains under substantial variations in scene scale and viewpoint.

paper_title: Series-wise Cross-validation for Global Time Series Forecasting
paper_abstract: We consider the problem of cross-validation (CV) in time series forecasting, with a focus on global forecasting models based on deep learning. The prevailing CV strategy in forecasting is to partition data across time with the last part of each series used for testing. With global models trained on collections of time series, however, a fundamentally different approach becomes possible: partitioning across series and time. We formalize series-wise CV for global forecasting models and benchmark several instantiations, including K-fold CV, bootstrapping, and Monte Carlo CV, on 11 datasets with 10 neural network architectures. We evaluate CV procedures along five dimensions: performance estimation, overoptimism rate, model selection accuracy, regret, and downstream forecasting performance. We withhold a random fraction of series from training so that they appear only in the test set. This protocol simulates the emergence of new series not seen during training, a common scenario in global forecasting. Under this protocol, our results reveal a nuanced trade-off: series-wise CV yields better downstream forecasting accuracy by guiding model selection toward configurations that generalize across both time and series, while time-wise CV retains a slight advantage for estimating out-of-sample error.

paper_title: Geometric Relevance Is Not Sufficient: Evaluating Focused Post-Training Supervision in Diffusion Docking
paper_abstract: Diffusion-based molecular docking requires learning a corrective score field across a broad corruption distribution, yet individual pose errors can differ substantially in their structural consequences. This creates a post-training conflict between preserving broad score-field coverage and concentrating supervision on corrections that appear more relevant to docking geometry. Using DiffDock, a fixed-budget study compares broad continuation with torsional supervision focused on Cartesian consequence or conditional target consistency, and with a broad/focused mixture. Evaluation separates fixed score fidelity, generated-pose quality, best-of-10 sampling capacity, and confidence-selected Top-1 docking performance. At <5 Angstrom, broad continuation had the highest mean Top-1 success among trained policies, and focused or mixed supervision showed no consistent advantage under the tested budget. The starting model had better fixed score fidelity, whereas the evaluated broad-continuation model had higher mean Top-1 success with the same aggregate best-of-10 recovery. Focusing supervision on structurally consequential or more consistently specified corrections did not consistently improve returned-pose success over broad continuation.
comments: 17 pages, 5 figures; accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 AI4DD Workshop

paper_title: ProQuant: Progressive Quantization-aware Training for Edge MLLMs
paper_abstract: Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) with impressive perception and understanding capabilities will enable a range of downstream applications. However, their substantial computational and memory requirements hinder the real-world implementation, particularly for resource-constrained edge devices. Quantization has emerged as an effective solution for deploying large models. While post-training quantization (PTQ) successfully retains the performance at moderate bit-width (e.g., W8A8), it suffers from severe performance degradation under low-bit quantization (e.g., W4A8), especially for small-scale models that are more suitable for edge deployment. In this paper, we propose ProQuant, a novel weight-activation quantization-aware training (QAT) framework tailored for low-bit MLLMs. First, to align the limited finetuning dataset distribution with the pretrained dataset distribution, we propose a self-relabeling (SRL) scheme to resample the responses of the open-source multimodal dataset. Second, we are the first to take a decoupled view of multi-modal (MM) understanding and language modeling abilities. We propose a progressive block activation (PBA) mechanism to prioritize the MM understanding recovery. We also introduce a vision-sensitive factor $\vecτ$ that effectively identifies the MM-critical layers. Extensive experiments across various benchmarks, covering models with 2B-8B parameters, show that ProQuant significantly outperforms existing methods. For example, our W4A8 Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct improves average accuracy by impressively 6.6% and achieves performance comparable to full precision counterparts with only approximately 1% performance drop. Code is available at https://github.com/yufeixue-ai/ProQuant/.

paper_title: BabyTheorist: A Benchmark for Learning to Theorize the World from Observation Alone
paper_abstract: How would we know whether a machine truly understands the world? We argue that one key capability is \textit{observational theory learning}: acquiring reusable theories from pure observations and applying them to new situations. Current visual reasoning benchmarks focus primarily on the latter, presenting each task as a few-shot puzzle grouped by a common rule. We introduce BabyTheorist, a benchmark for controlled training and evaluation of observational theory learning. BabyTheorist generates continual streams of before-after visual observations from hidden compositional programs; during training, learners see only the resulting transitions, with no program labels, task identities, or support sets. To support theory learning and evaluation, BabyTheorist controls the program language, a curriculum over program complexity, recurring frequent subprograms, and a continual train-test protocol with level skipping. Seven representative baselines plateau well below ceiling, with the gap widening as the curriculum advances---evidence that BabyTheorist isolates a capability current program-learning approaches do not yet address.

paper_title: A Generative Foundation Model for Multimodal Tokamak Tasks
paper_abstract: Tokamak experiments record diverse measurements, including waveforms, profiles, fields, and scalars, which are used to reconstruct the plasma, forecast its evolution, recover associated control signals, and estimate disruption risk. Most models are built separately for one task and a fixed set of inputs and outputs, and each relies on a prescribed subset of diagnostics rather than structuring the full multimodal observation set to extract global, cross-signal information about the discharge. These limitations motivate a reusable foundation model that adapts to each task's input-output schema and models heterogeneous target signals jointly, rather than retraining a separate model for every configuration. In this work, we extend the TokaMark benchmark with two groups of tasks for actuator action inversion and disruption prediction, yielding 20 MAST tasks in six groups with explicit schemas and evaluation protocols. Then, we introduce GenToka, a generative tokamak foundation model that jointly generates schema-selected targets through a shared conditional diffusion Transformer, with signal-specific codecs preserving native time series, profiles, fields, and scalars; foundation pretraining and task-specific adaptation transfer cross-signal structure across all six groups. Evaluation on MAST measurements shows that GenToka reduces macro-average normalized root mean squared error relative to TokaMind by 4.7% on Groups 1-4 and by 17.7% on Group 5, and improves macro-average window-level F1 on Group 6 by 8.4% at a common validation-selected threshold. GenToka provides a reusable, generative, and multimodal pathway for experimental tokamaks, linking plasma-state reconstruction, actuator inference, and disruption warning from shared measurements to support more integrated, data-driven fusion plasma prediction and control research.

paper_title: Who Can Evaluate AI Independently? A Framework for Analysing Evaluation Infrastructure
paper_abstract: AI evaluation is increasingly central to AI safety and governance, yet taking part in an evaluation does not by itself confer authority over its design, its execution or the resources it depends on. This paper examines how infrastructure arrangements distribute that authority, and so shape who can evaluate AI systems independently.
